# Super-Sample Covariance

This page describes the super-sample covariance (SSC) matrix $S_{ij}$ computed by
[[numcosmo|NcXcorSSCSij]], and how it enters the Gaussian cluster number-count
likelihood [[numcosmo|NcDataClusterNCountsGauss]].

## The effect

A survey measures a finite volume, so density modes with wavelengths longer than
the footprint are not observable. They are not harmless: they shift the mean
density inside the volume away from the cosmic mean, and every count drawn from
that volume responds to the shift. Writing $\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}$ for the mean
matter density contrast over redshift bin $i$, the expected counts respond
linearly through the halo bias $b_i$,
$$
N_i = \bar{N}_i \left(1 + b_i\,\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}\right),
$$
and since $\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}$ is itself a random variable the counts acquire
a covariance beyond the Poisson one,
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(N_i, N_j) = \bar{N}_i\,\delta_{ij} + b_i b_j\,S_{ij},
\qquad
S_{ij} \equiv \left\langle \delta_{\mathrm{b},i}\,\delta_{\mathrm{b},j} \right\rangle .
$$
The first term is the shot noise; the second is the super-sample term. Because
the same long-wavelength modes cover every bin, $S_{ij}$ is not diagonal: it
correlates bins that do not overlap in redshift at all. See
@TakadaHu2013 and @LacasaGrain2019 for the derivation of the effect
and of the estimator used here.

## $S_{ij}$ as an angular power spectrum

The bin-averaged contrast $\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}$ is the matter contrast smoothed
by the survey window: a top hat in the radial direction over bin $i$, and the
survey footprint on the sky. Separating the two, $S_{ij}$ becomes a sum over
multipoles of the angular power spectrum $C^{ij}_\ell$ of the radially averaged
contrast.

Define the radial window of bin $i$ to be a top hat normalized to unit integral
in comoving volume, so that $\delta_{\mathrm{b},i}$ is a plain volume average and
not a weighted one. Then, for a full-sky survey, only the monopole survives,
$$
S_{ij} = \frac{C^{ij}_0}{4\pi} .
$$

For a real footprint, described by a mask $W(\hat{n})$ with angular power
spectrum $C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell$ and sky fraction
$f_{\mathrm{sky}} = \sqrt{C^{\mathrm{mask}}_0 / 4\pi}$, the mask couples
multipoles and the estimator becomes
$$
S_{ij} = \frac{1}{\left(4\pi f_{\mathrm{sky}}\right)^2}
  \sum_{\ell=0}^{\ell_{\max}} (2\ell+1)\,C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell\,C^{ij}_\ell .
$$

Substituting $f_{\mathrm{sky}}^2 = C^{\mathrm{mask}}_0 / 4\pi$ removes the square
root and gives the form actually evaluated,
$$
S_{ij} = \frac{1}{4\pi\,C^{\mathrm{mask}}_0}
  \sum_{\ell=0}^{\ell_{\max}} (2\ell+1)\,C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell\,C^{ij}_\ell .
$$

The full-sky case is not a separate branch of this expression but the special
value $C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell = 4\pi\,\delta_{\ell 0}$, for which the sum
collapses to $C^{ij}_0 / 4\pi$. [[numcosmo|NcXcorSSCSij]] uses that spectrum as
its default footprint, so full sky and masked runs share one code path.

### Finite area, and a trap

Between the two extremes sits the estimator an analysis quoting only a survey
area uses: the full-sky matrix rescaled by the sky fraction,
$$
S_{ij} = \frac{S^{\rm fullsky}_{ij}}{f_{\rm sky}},
\qquad f_{\rm sky} = \frac{\Omega}{4\pi} .
$$
It is a crude correction rather than a mask deconvolution — it knows the solid
angle of the footprint but nothing about its shape — yet it captures the effect
that actually dominates: a smaller volume samples fewer long-wavelength modes,
so the background density fluctuates more. It costs a single multipole, like the
full-sky case. `nc_xcor_ssc_sij_set_area()` selects it.

**Using the plain full-sky $S_{ij}$ for a survey that does not cover the full
sky is a mistake, not a conservative approximation.** With
$f_{\rm sky} < 1$ the rescaling only ever increases $S_{ij}$, so omitting it
understates the super-sample variance, and the resulting parameter constraints
come out too tight. The size of the error is $1/f_{\rm sky}$ — a factor of
about $2.3$ for $18\,000\ \mathrm{deg}^2$, and about $14$ for
$3\,000\ \mathrm{deg}^2$. A finite survey needs either an area or a mask.

The truncation $\ell_{\max}$ is set by how much of the mask variance
$\sum_\ell (2\ell+1) C^{\mathrm{mask}}_\ell / 4\pi$ must be recovered; the
`find_lmax` helper in `numcosmo_py.ssc` picks the smallest value meeting a
requested tolerance.

## Why the Limber approximation cannot be used

The Limber approximation replaces the spherical Bessel functions in the radial
integral by a delta function, which is accurate only when the window is broad
compared with the oscillation scale — that is, at high $\ell$. Here the sum is
dominated by the very lowest multipoles, $\ell = 0$ for a full-sky survey, where
Limber is meaningless. Worse, it makes the cross spectrum of two bins with
disjoint redshift support vanish identically, whereas the true $C^{ij}_\ell$ is
non-zero: two disjoint shells are windows on the same three-dimensional field,
and the non-Limber calculation couples them through the outer $k$ integral rather
than through a shared $z$ integral.

[[numcosmo|NcXcorSSCSij]] therefore puts every kernel in permanent non-Limber
mode, and the radial integrals are done with the spherical-Bessel machinery of
[[numcosmo|NcXcorSolver]].

## Numerical accuracy

The off-diagonal $S_{ij}$ of well-separated bins are a small residual of a large
cancellation: for seven top-hat bins over $z \in [0.1, 0.8]$, $|S_{06}|$ is four
orders of magnitude below $S_{00}$. Their accuracy is set by `scaled-abstol`, the
absolute floor of the adaptive refinement building the $U_i(k)$ spline, and
**not** by `reltol`, which is inactive while `scaled-abstol` binds. Measured
against a converged independent quadrature:

| `scaled-abstol`               | $S_{00}$ | $S_{01}$ | $S_{04}$ | $S_{06}$ |
|-------------------------------|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|
| $10^{-4}$ ([[numcosmo\|NcXcorKernel]] default) |  $-0.07\%$ |  $-0.59\%$ | $-19.6\%$ | $-59.1\%$ |
| $10^{-6}$ ([[numcosmo\|NcXcorSSCSij]] default) | $0.006\%$ | $-0.014\%$ |  $0.28\%$ |  $-5.2\%$ |
| $10^{-8}$                     | $0.001\%$ | $-0.003\%$ |  $0.02\%$ | $-0.06\%$ |

The residual at $10^{-8}$ is consistent with the reference's own convergence
rather than with a NumCosmo error. It is not the default because the adaptive
cubature can run out of Clenshaw–Curtis levels at that setting on masked runs and
abort, which is fatal inside a Monte Carlo chain. For the same reason the default
quadrature is `NC_XCOR_METHOD_KERNEL_FIXED`, an exact Gauss–Legendre rule on the
union of the pair's spline knots: it targets no tolerance, so it cannot fail to
reach one.

## Varying $S_{ij}$ along a chain

$S_{ij}$ depends on cosmology, like every other part of the covariance. A
reference analysis may still hold it at a fiducial value and vary only the mean
and the Poisson term, which is much cheaper: recomputing $S_{ij}$ per likelihood
step costs about $+60\%$ over the rest of the evaluation for a full-sky or
area-rescaled footprint, and roughly a factor of six for a masked one, where
every multipole up to $\ell_{\max}$ must be solved.

Setting [[numcosmo|NcDataClusterNCountsGauss]]:ssc-sij replaces the fixed matrix
by a calculator invoked at every prepare, which is what justifies the frozen
approximation rather than assuming it: run both and compare the posteriors.

Two conditions make that comparison meaningful.

**The normalization must be kept.** For a Gaussian likelihood,
$$
-2\ln L = \left(N - \bar{N}\right)^\mathsf{T} C^{-1} \left(N - \bar{N}\right)
        + \ln \det C + n \ln 2\pi ,
$$
and the $\ln \det C$ term is constant only while $C$ is. Once the covariance
varies with cosmology, dropping it biases the posterior towards high-variance
cosmologies — exactly the direction in which a varying $S_{ij}$ moves. The
`use-norma` property of [[numcosmo-math|NcmDataGaussCov]] controls that term, and
[[numcosmo|NcDataClusterNCountsGauss]] refuses to begin with a varying $S_{ij}$
unless it is set.

**The mock must not move.** Only the fitting covariance may follow the
cosmology; the matrix used while resampling stays the one given to
`nc_data_cluster_ncounts_gauss_set_resample_s_matrix()`, so the fixed and varying
analyses fit the same realization and differ only in what is being tested.
